extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers studying U.S. government and constitutional law
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation of the President's election procedures, succession, impeachment, and enumerated powers and duties under the Constitution and statute, with historical examples and commentary on practical effects and dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral majority requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution requires for the choice of a President "a majority of the whole number of electors appointed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no candidate receives an absolute majority of electoral votes (example given: in 1912 total electors 529, absolute majority 265), the choice goes to the House of Representatives. The text provides numeric examples and stresses the constitutional textual requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: House selection when no electoral majority
rubrics_metrics.description: If no candidate attains an absolute majority of electoral votes, the House chooses a President from among the three candidates who have received the largest number of electoral votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the House the vote is taken by States and a majority of all the States is necessary for a choice; if a State delegation is equally divided its collective vote is lost. Historical examples: the elections of 1800 and 1824 illustrate consequences and potential divergence from popular will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting and admissibility of electoral votes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution seems to have intended to leave the counting of the votes to the president of the Senate, but Congress has assumed the right to determine all questions regarding the validity of electoral votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This congressional role has produced partisan determinations and deadlocks. The 1876 crisis and subsequent remedies (1887 statute) are discussed: statutes now provide that state tribunals determine which electoral votes are legal; if none exist the two Houses decide, and if the Houses differ the State's vote is lost. The entry emphasises problems of uncertainty and partisan decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradition of two presidential terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A long-standing tradition (originating with Washington's refusal to serve a third term) that Presidents not seek more than two terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes how this tradition constrained later presidents and conventions (examples: Washington refusing third term; attempts to renominate Grant in 1880; Roosevelt in 1912). It emphasises that the tradition is powerful though not legally binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of electoral commissions for disputed returns
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of double returns, a specially created electoral commission may determine admissibility of returns (example: 1876 statute creating a commission of 5 Senators, 5 Representatives, and 5 Supreme Court Justices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition of such a commission can determine outcome; commissioners often vote along party lines despite oaths of impartiality. The 1876 commission’s 8–7 partisan decisions that elected Hayes are used to illustrate risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment procedure and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A President is removable during his term only by means of impeachment: the House impeaches, and the Senate, sitting as a law court with the Chief Justice presiding, tries the case; a two-thirds vote is necessary to convict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conviction removes and disqualifies from office but leaves the individual liable to ordinary indictment and punishment. Impeachable offences are 'treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanours' — the scope of which is debated (some limiting to indictable offences, others extending to violations of official duty). Historical example: Andrew Johnson's impeachment and acquittal are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential succession rules
rubrics_metrics.description: On removal by impeachment, death, resignation, or inability to discharge duties, the Vice‑President succeeds to the Presidency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, when both President and Vice‑President were lacking a statute provided succession via presiding officer of the Senate and then the Speaker; by an Act of 1886 succession was reordered so the Secretary of State succeeds and then other officers by rank. Examples of Presidents dying in office and Vice‑Presidents succeeding are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vice‑President functions and selection practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vice‑President is chosen at the same time and by the same electors as the President; his functions are to preside in the Senate and to succeed the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice little pains are often taken over selecting a Vice‑President: conventions may nominate a second‑rank man to placate factions, reward contributors, console disappointed candidates, or 'shelve' someone. If the President dies, a potentially politically weak or different‑minded Vice‑President may assume the Presidency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated presidential powers and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The powers and duties of the President include: command of the Federal army and navy and of state militias when called; power to make treaties (with Senate advice and consent — two‑thirds); appoint ambassadors, consuls, Supreme Court judges and other higher federal officers (with Senate advice and consent); grant reprieves and pardons for offences against the United States except in cases of impeachment; convene both Houses on extraordinary occasions; return (veto) bills; duty to inform Congress of the State of the Union and recommend measures; commission all officers; receive foreign ambassadors; and take care that the laws be faithfully executed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list is explicit in the text and is later grouped into four classes. The veto rules (return within ten days; two‑thirds override; pocket veto if Congress adjourns) are included as part of these duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping of presidential functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The President's functions cluster into four classes: those relating to foreign affairs; those relating to domestic administration; those concerning legislation; and the power of appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy is offered to clarify the different spheres in which presidential powers operate and to structure discussion of limits and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and practice in foreign policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The President has primary initiative in foreign affairs but cannot declare war (that power belongs to Congress); treaties require the advice and consent of two‑thirds of the Senate; the House has no legal right to interfere but may pass resolutions expressing opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical politics requires the Executive to communicate with the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee to secure treaty approval; the President or his Secretary of State retains an unfettered initiative and can embroil the country abroad, while the Senate can prevent actions but cannot necessarily keep the Executive from unsettling matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of executive authority in wartime
rubrics_metrics.description: The President's direct domestic authority is small in peace but expands rapidly in wartime, when as commander‑in‑chief and guardian of law execution he may assume extraordinary powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples include Lincoln's suspension of the writ of habeas corpus and his emancipation proclamations, acts later legalized by Congress. The text notes dispute over how much the President can legally do without prior legislative sanction and that Congress can (by statute) make the President nearly dictatorial in wartime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarantee of republican government and use of federal force
rubrics_metrics.description: It devolves on the executive as well as on Congress to give effect to the constitutional guarantee of a republican form of government to each State; on application of a State's legislature or executive, the federal government may protect against domestic violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President may employ troops or militia to restore government or protect order (examples: Louisiana 1873, Rhode Island 1840–2, Illinois 1894). The text stresses the rarity but importance of this power and notes judicial limitations (e.g., Luther v. Borden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to address the nation
rubrics_metrics.description: The President has the right to speak to the nation by addresses or proclamations, a right not expressly conferred by the Constitution but inherent in his position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasions for such addresses are uncommon; customary examples include the inaugural address and the duty to inform Congress (State of the Union). The text remarks on norms of presidential public speaking (e.g., avoiding partisan stump tours) and notes the President retains ordinary citizen rights (including voting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role in legislation: recommendation versus initiation
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is not a member of either House and cannot directly introduce bills; his constitutional role in legislation is to inform Congress of the state of the Union and to recommend measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presidential messages discuss leading questions and suggest requisite legislation; administration‑drafted bills may be introduced by sympathetic members, but without ministers in Congress these messages may be only manifestos. The President's most effective legislative power is at the final stage (signing or vetoing bills).

rubrics_metrics.name: Veto power mechanics and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When a bill is presented the President may sign it into law or return it within ten days to the originating House with grounds of disapproval; if both Houses pass the bill again by a two‑thirds majority in each, it becomes law without his signature. If Congress adjourns within the ten days, the bill is lost (pocket veto).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically Presidents have used the veto sparingly except in certain periods (Jackson, Cleveland). The provision was deliberately included despite its apparent undemocratic character, and has generally worked well as a constitutional check.

rubrics_metrics.name: High stakes of presidential contests and risk of state‑level fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Because electoral ballots are received and counted by State authorities under state laws and the stakes for the Presidency are very high, unscrupulous state factions have opportunities for fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 1876 contested election is used to illustrate how high stakes lead parties to claim disputed returns and exploit state mechanisms. The text argues that some institutional reforms (e.g., state tribunals, federal statutes) are preferable to uncertainty even if imperfect.
